question: Which three aims is a flight management system designed for?

options.text: Engine monitoring, fire detection, less maintenance
Better radio range, cabin comfort, less noise
Better navigation, fuel efficiency, less workload
Collision avoidance, terrain warning, crew alerting

explanation: An FMS is designed to improve navigation, aid fuel efficiency and reduce crew workload, flying complex routes and profiles automatically.

question: What does LNAV provide?

options.text: Lateral guidance along the route
Guidance for the landing flare
Speed guidance on the approach
Vertical guidance in climb and descent

explanation: LNAV is lateral navigation: steering commands to fly the aircraft along the route. VNAV provides the vertical profile and speeds.

question: What does VNAV enable the FMS to calculate?

options.text: The cross-track error on the approach
The aircraft's position from the radio aids along the route
Wind and drift from the inertial data
Optimum levels and climb and descent speeds

explanation: Vertical navigation lets the system calculate optimum cruise altitudes and the best combination of thrust and speed during the climb and descent.

question: How is the FMS control unit sometimes described?

options.text: A back-up for the standby instruments
A miniature flight deck with fingertip control
A recorder of the aircraft's flight path for later analysis
A display of engine parameters

explanation: When the crew are not flying by hand they use the FMS controls to fly the aircraft, so the control unit acts as a miniature flight deck with fingertip control.

question: Which units feed a typical FMS with navigation and air data?

options.text: The IRS, ADC and GPS
The GPWS, ACAS and weather radar only
The FDR, CVR and ELT
The engine and fuel computers only

explanation: The FMC takes position from the IRS and GPS (and radio aids) and air data from the ADC, and sends its commands to the flight guidance system.

question: What is the primary function of the FMS control and display unit?

options.text: The storage of the navigation database
The display of the moving map
The calculation of thrust commands
The crew's interface with the system

explanation: The CDU is the crew's interface with the FMS. Through it the crew can command fully automatic, semi-automatic or manual operation.

question: Where are the two FMS control units usually fitted?

options.text: Above the windscreen in the overhead panel
Either side of the centre console
In front of each pilot below the glareshield
Behind the pilots' seats

explanation: Two CDUs are usually fitted either side of the centre console, with the left one normally the master. Some aircraft have a third CDU for engineering use.

question: In a dual FMS installation, which control unit is normally the master?

options.text: The one last used
The right one
The left one
The third, centre one

explanation: The left CDU is normally the master. A third CDU, where fitted, is placed on the centre console mainly for engineering staff.

question: What does an FMS control unit display data on?

options.text: A screen of pages, with a key panel
A paper printer and keyboard
A row of fixed numerical windows only
The primary flight display only

explanation: The CDU has a monochrome or colour screen on which different pages of data can be shown, together with a selector key panel.

question: What is the normal operating mode of a dual FMC installation?

options.text: Standby mode
Dual mode
Independent mode
Single mode

explanation: In dual mode, the norm, both FMCs process entries from both CDUs and compare results so that crucial data is consistent; the same output then goes to both.

question: In dual mode, what do the two FMCs do with pilot entries?

options.text: They take turns, changing over each hour
Each processes only its own side's entries
One processes them, the other stays off-line
Both process them and compare the results

explanation: Both FMCs independently process entries from both CDUs and compare the results. This cross-check ensures the critical information is the same in both.

question: Why is independent mode not the usual way to operate the FMCs?

options.text: It disconnects the autopilot
It doubles the fuel used
There is no cross-check
It needs a third control unit on the centre console

explanation: The FMCs can be decoupled into fully independent operation, but then neither checks the other, so it is not normal practice.

question: What is single mode in an FMS?

options.text: Both FMCs working without comparing results
One FMC working alone after the other fails
Operation with only one control unit fitted
Operation with the database switched off

explanation: If one FMC fails, the other can be expected to operate the aircraft successfully on its own. The failed FMC may be selected out to allow this.

question: Into which two major sections is the FMC database divided?

options.text: Lateral and vertical guidance
Engines and airframe
Performance and navigation
Fuel and weight

explanation: The database has a performance section (drag, engine data, speeds) and a navigation section (navaids, airports, runways and procedures).

question: What is the purpose of the FMC performance database?

options.text: To give the data for pitch and thrust commands
To record the aircraft's performance in flight
To store the routes and waypoints
To hold the take-off and landing charts only

explanation: It reduces the crew's need to look things up in the cruise manual and gives the FMC the data it needs to calculate pitch and thrust commands.

question: Which data is held in the FMC performance database?

options.text: The flight number, the crew names and the company route
Company routes and SIDs
Navaid positions and runway lengths
Drag, engine data and limit speeds

explanation: The performance database holds aircraft drag and engine characteristics and maximum and minimum speeds. Maintenance can refine it with drag and fuel flow factors.

question: How can maintenance tailor the performance database to an individual aircraft?

options.text: By deleting the cost index function from the software
By loading a new engine type
By changing its maximum speeds
By entering drag and fuel flow factors

explanation: An individual aircraft drifts away from the published figures as it ages, so maintenance enters factors for drag and fuel flow that refine the predictions for that airframe.

question: Which information is held in the FMC navigation database?

options.text: Navaids, airports, procedures and routes
The aircraft's maintenance history
Weather forecasts for the route
Aircraft drag, engine characteristics and limit speeds

explanation: It holds most of the information normally read from navigation charts: navaid and airport locations, runways, and airline-selected data such as SIDs, STARs, approaches and company routes.

question: How many sets of navigation data does the FMC hold, and for how long is each valid?

options.text: Three sets, each valid for one year
Two sets, each valid for 56 days
Two sets, each valid for 28 days
One set, valid for 28 days

explanation: The FMC holds two sets of navigation data, each matching a 28-day chart revision cycle. The crew selects the active one during preflight.

question: Who updates the FMC navigation database, and how often?

options.text: The crew, before every flight
Maintenance, every 28 days
The crew, every 7 days
Maintenance, once a year

explanation: Maintenance loads the new data every 28 days, so when the chart revision date arrives the new set is already in the FMC, ready to select.

question: Which navigation data set does the FMC use for its calculations?

options.text: The active set, chosen by the crew
Always the newer of the two sets
Both sets, averaged together
The set loaded most recently by maintenance

explanation: During preflight the crew selects which of the two sets is active, and the FMC uses that set for navigation calculations.

question: What does the FMS do first when power is applied?

options.text: It shows the route page for the last flight
It self-tests, then shows IDENT
It asks for the cost index
It starts aligning the IRS automatically

explanation: On power-up the FMS executes a self-test; once it completes successfully the IDENT page is displayed.

question: Which important check is made on the IDENT page?

options.text: The flight number, the route and the cruise altitude
The fuel quantity in each tank
The IRS alignment status
The database in use and its validity

explanation: The IDENT page confirms the aircraft details and the navigation database in operation, with the date of changeover to the next cycle. It prompts if the database is out of date.

question: Why is the FMS clock checked against the aircraft clock on the POS INIT page?

options.text: The clock sets the navigation database cycle
The clock controls the fuel calculations only
ETAs and recorded data must match
The FMS clock drives the IRS alignment

explanation: Data is saved on the flight data recorder against time, and the FMC's ETAs must match the aircraft clock, so the two must be synchronised.

question: Which position is entered on the POS INIT page for IRS alignment?

options.text: The first waypoint of the route
The gate position
The destination airport position from the route
The position of the nearest VOR

explanation: The gate position, or the airfield datum if no gate position exists, is entered accurately for IRS alignment. It is often updated at the take-off point.

question: Why may the FMS position be updated at the take-off point?

options.text: Because the IRS loses alignment while taxiing
Because the gate position is not accepted
To reset the database to the active cycle
To give the best initial position for flight

explanation: The gate position is good enough for alignment, but updating at the runway gives the best possible starting position for the flight.

question: Which entries are made on the RTE page?

options.text: The database identifier and the drag and fuel flow factors
Fuel, weights and cruise altitude
Airports, flight number and route
IRS position and heading reference

explanation: On the RTE page the crew enters the departure and destination airport codes, the flight number and a company route, then activates it.

question: Which data is entered on the PERF INIT page?

options.text: Weights, fuel, cost index and level
IRS position and the time zone
Origin and destination airports and the flight number
The navigation database cycle

explanation: PERF INIT updates the aircraft's performance and weight configuration: gross weight or zero fuel weight, fuel, reserves, cost index, cruise altitude and step size.

question: On which FMS page is the drag and fuel flow factor shown?

options.text: RTE
PERF INIT
POS INIT
IDENT

explanation: The IDENT page shows the aeroplane model, operational programme, drag and fuel flow factors, and the navigation database identifier and cycle.

question: On which FMS page are the IRS position and heading references found?

options.text: POS INIT
IDENT
PERF INIT
RTE

explanation: POS INIT gives the IRS position reference, the IRS heading reference and the GMT/UTC time display.

question: On which FMS page is the zero fuel weight entered?

options.text: POS INIT
PERF INIT
RTE
IDENT

explanation: The PERF INIT page takes the gross weight, fuel quantity, zero fuel weight, reserves, cost index, cruise altitude and step size.

question: What does a cost index of zero give?

options.text: Minimum trip time: maximum speed
The lowest cruise altitude
Minimum fuel: maximum range
Long range cruise with a fast descent

explanation: A cost index of zero gives economy speeds for minimum fuel: maximum range cruise and a low-speed descent.

question: How is the cost index calculated?

options.text: Trip distance ÷ fuel burn
Fuel cost per unit ÷ operating cost per hour
Fuel cost × operating cost per hour
Operating cost per hour ÷ fuel cost

explanation: Cost index = aeroplane operating cost per hour ÷ fuel cost per unit. A high index means time is expensive, so the FMC flies faster.

question: An operator's time costs are high compared with fuel. What cost index and speed will result?

options.text: A cost index of zero and maximum speed
A high cost index and higher speeds
A cost index of zero and maximum range
A low cost index and lower speeds

explanation: Cost index rises when time costs rise relative to fuel. A higher index makes the FMC fly faster, burning more fuel to save time.

question: How does a higher selected speed affect trip costs?

options.text: Higher fuel cost, lower time cost
Lower fuel and lower time cost
Higher fuel and higher time cost
Lower fuel cost, higher time cost

explanation: The faster the aircraft flies in climb, cruise or descent, the more fuel it burns, but the less time-related cost it incurs.

question: Which cruise mode gives the lowest operating cost for the entered cost index?

options.text: Selected speed cruise
Long range cruise
Economy cruise
Maximum range cruise

explanation: Economy cruise uses the cost index to balance fuel and time and so yields the lowest operating cost. Maximum range is the special case of a zero index.

question: What vertical profile does the FMC command in a VNAV climb?

options.text: Take-off thrust all the way to cruise level
Maximum continuous thrust at the lowest manoeuvring speed
Climb thrust, SID limits, then economy speed
Idle thrust at a fixed rate of climb

explanation: The VNAV climb uses climb thrust, staying within the SID's speed and altitude constraints, then climbs at economy speed to the entered cruise altitude.

question: In a VNAV climb, when is UNABLE NEXT ALT displayed?

options.text: When an altitude constraint will be missed
When the autothrottle is disconnected
When the next waypoint has no altitude
When the cruise altitude is above the aircraft's ceiling

explanation: If flying the climb speed profile would violate an altitude constraint, UNABLE NEXT ALT is shown. The pilot then selects a lower speed giving a steeper climb.

question: After UNABLE NEXT ALT, what should the pilot select?

options.text: Independent FMC mode
A higher cruise altitude on the CDU
A higher cost index
A speed giving a steeper climb angle

explanation: The pilot must choose a different speed on the CDU that gives a steeper climb angle, usually closer to the best angle of climb speed.

question: Until when may the cruise speed mode be changed, for example to LRC?

options.text: Only before take-off
Until passing the top of descent
Only until the top of climb
Until the final approach fix is passed

explanation: A number of cost index modifications, such as long range cruise or a selected speed, are allowed until passing the top of descent point.

question: What kind of tracks does LNAV normally fly between waypoints?

options.text: Grid tracks
Rhumb line tracks
Constant magnetic headings
Great circle tracks

explanation: LNAV guidance between the waypoints of the active route is normally along great circle tracks.

question: When a stored procedure is in the active route, what else can LNAV fly?

options.text: A heading, a track or a DME arc
Only great circle tracks
Only radials to and from the VORs on the route
Only rhumb line tracks

explanation: For procedures in the database the FMC can command a constant heading, a track or a DME arc, as the procedure requires.

question: From which systems does the FMC determine its present position?

options.text: The radio altimeter and the ILS
IRS, DME, VOR and GPS
The flux valve and the standby compass
The air data computer only

explanation: The FMC combines inputs from the IRS/INS, DME, VOR, GPS and any other navigation systems fitted, and steers along the active leg from that position.

question: What is the minimum position input the FMC needs to function?

options.text: A VOR and a DME
At least two DME stations
At least one IRS or INS
A GPS receiver

explanation: The FMC requires position information from at least one IRS or INS. Radio and satellite updates improve it but are not essential.

question: On the ground, how does the FMC calculate present position?

options.text: From DME and VOR updates
From the GPS only
From the gate position alone, with no IRS
From the IRS or INS only

explanation: While the aircraft is on the ground the FMC uses only the IRS or INS for present position.

question: Why does the FMC position slowly accumulate error?

options.text: Inertial positions drift with time
The database loses accuracy during the flight
The FMC clock gains time
The GPS is switched off in cruise

explanation: The FMC position is normally a combination of the IRS/INS positions, and inertial systems accumulate error with time. Comparing the individual IRS positions on the CDU reveals it.

question: After a long ground delay, a significant map error is seen. What should be done?

options.text: Increase the cost index
Select the other navigation database on IDENT
Realign the IRS and re-enter position
Change to independent FMC mode

explanation: Inertial errors grow with time even on the ground. If a significant map error is noticed after an extended delay, the IRS/INS should be realigned and the position re-entered.

question: What is the FMS End of Descent (E/D) point?

options.text: The point where the descent begins
A constrained waypoint at the FAF or threshold
The missed approach point
The lowest altitude reached in the hold

explanation: The E/D is a waypoint with an altitude and airspeed constraint that coincides with the final approach fix or the runway threshold. The descent path is built back from it.

question: On what does the FMC base its descent path for a programmed arrival?

options.text: The arrival's constraints and the E/D
A fixed 3° path from top of descent
The radio altitude and the glide slope
The cruise altitude and the cost index alone, with no constraints

explanation: When an arrival is entered, the FMC builds a descent path to meet the procedure's airspeed and altitude constraints and the end of descent point.

question: For a non-precision approach, to which point is the FMC computed path built?

options.text: The missed approach point at the minimum descent altitude
50 ft over the runway threshold
The decision height
The touchdown zone at 0 ft

explanation: For VFR and non-precision approaches the computed path ends 50 ft over the approach end of the runway. The crew must not descend below the minima without visual contact.

question: During a missed approach, what LNAV guidance is available?

options.text: None; LNAV disconnects at the missed approach
Guidance to the alternate aerodrome only
To the missed approach point
Guidance back to the departure aerodrome

explanation: LNAV guidance remains available during a missed approach to the missed approach point and altitude.

question: What radial error rate is not uncommon for a modern FMS?

options.text: About 2 NM per hour
About 0.5 NM per minute of flight
About 5 NM per hour
Under 0.05 NM per hour

explanation: With combined inertial and radio inputs, radial error rates below 0.05 NM per hour are not uncommon. GPS input improves performance further.

question: Which factor remains decisive for FMS accuracy, however good the system?

options.text: The colour of the CDU display
Operator skill and monitoring
The age of the IRS units
The number of FMC units fitted to the aircraft

explanation: GPS and multiple sensors improve accuracy, but the skill of the operator and constant, careful monitoring always remain a deciding factor.

question: On the FMS control unit, what does the white MSG annunciator indicate?

options.text: A message is waiting
The page is not the active leg
The FMC has failed
A parallel offset is in use

explanation: MSG illuminates white when there is an alerting or advisory message, or messages pending, in the scratchpad.

question: What colour is the FAIL annunciator on the FMS control unit, and what does it mean?

options.text: White: a message is waiting
White: a parallel offset is active
Red: the database is out of date
Amber: an FMC has failed

explanation: FAIL illuminates amber when an FMC failure is detected. MSG, DSPY and OFST are white.

question: When does the DSPY (display) annunciator illuminate?

options.text: When the database is about to expire
When the display has failed
When the page is not the active one
When the FMC is in independent mode

explanation: DSPY lights white if the displayed page is not related to the active flight plan leg or to the current performance mode, reminding the crew they are viewing something else.

question: What does the OFST annunciator on the FMS control unit show?

options.text: The FMC has lost its IRS input
The aircraft is off the active route
A position update is needed
A parallel offset is in use

explanation: OFST lights white when the aircraft is flying a parallel offset: parallel to the planned track but a fixed distance from it.
